# When and how to refer

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D11 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.1

## You will be able to

- Apply the basic rule: an abnormal or suspicious screen leads to fetal echocardiography.
- List the fetal findings that are indications for fetal echocardiography.
- List the maternal and family factors that are indications.
- Tell apart factors where echocardiography may be considered and factors with insufficient evidence.
- Say who should perform the fetal echocardiogram and what counselling must take into account.

## The basic rule

A fetus with a known or suspected abnormality on cardiac screening is a candidate for fetal echocardiography. [1]

Screening programmes with a low threshold for referral perform better. [2]

You do not need a diagnosis to refer. 'One plane did not meet its criteria' is reason enough.


## Risk factors add to screening; they do not replace it

When there is a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease, fetal echocardiography is indicated in addition to routine screening. How this is arranged depends on local resources, the setting, the availability of examiners and the screening results. [3]

A high proportion of detectable heart disease occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor and no other anomaly. A clean history never excuses a poor screen. [4]


## Fetal indications

The guideline lists these fetal factors as common indications for fetal echocardiography. [5]

| Fetal factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Suspected structural heart anomaly |  |
| Extracardiac anomaly | Of a kind associated with heart disease |
| Suspected abnormal function or a large heart |  |
| Hydrops |  |
| Persistent tachycardia | 180 beats per minute or more |
| Suspected heart block or persistent bradycardia | 110 beats per minute or less |
| Irregular rhythm | Frequent or persistent |
| Increased nuchal translucency | 3.5 mm or more |
| Genetic abnormality | Confirmed or suspected |
| Monochorionic twins | If resources allow |

A nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more at 11 to 14 weeks remains an indication even if the measurement later becomes normal. [6]


## Findings on the screen that should not be passed

Right-left asymmetry of the ventricles in mid-gestation warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return. [7]

A major difference in size between the two great arteries should lead to further evaluation. [8]

An abnormal cardiac axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly. [9]

If the heart or the stomach is not on the left, suspect a situs abnormality. [10]


## Maternal and family indications

The guideline lists these maternal, family and exposure factors as common indications. [11]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative of the fetus |  |
| Mendelian disease with childhood cardiac manifestations | In a first- or second-degree relative |
| Pregestational diabetes | Whatever the HbA1c |
| Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies |  |
| Phenylketonuria | Unknown status, or periconceptional phenylalanine above 10 mg/dL |
| Retinoid exposure |  |
| Confirmed fetal infection | TORCH or parvovirus B19 |


## May be considered

For some factors the guideline says fetal echocardiography may be considered. [12]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Congenital heart disease in a second-degree relative |  |
| Gestational diabetes | Diagnosed in the first or early second trimester |
| Nuchal translucency | 3.0 to 3.4 mm |
| Selected teratogens | For example paroxetine, carbamazepine, lithium, sodium valproate |
| Conception by IVF | Including ICSI |
| ACE inhibitor use |  |


## Not enough evidence of raised risk

For these factors the guideline finds insufficient evidence that risk is significantly above baseline. It does not list them as indications for fetal echocardiography. [13]

| Factor | Detail |
|---|---|
| Obesity | BMI 35 or more |
| SSRI exposure | Other than paroxetine |
| Non-cardiac soft markers |  |
| Abnormal serum analytes |  |
| Single umbilical artery | Isolated |
| Gestational diabetes | Diagnosed after the second trimester |
| Warfarin or alcohol exposure |  |
| Echogenic intracardiac focus |  |
| Fever, or viral infection with seroconversion only |  |
| Heart disease in a distant relative | Isolated; more distant than second degree |

These patients still need a careful routine screen, like everyone else.


## Who does the echocardiogram, and what families need

Fetal echocardiography is best performed by a trained specialist who knows both prenatal diagnosis and the course after birth. [14]

Counselling after a heart problem is detected should take into account the high prevalence of psychological distress in the mother. [14]

Findings on the three-vessel views can change what happens next: testing for 22q11 microdeletion, the planned place of delivery as in complete transposition, readiness to give prostaglandin, or readiness for airway problems from vascular compression. [15]

## Before you close the report: refer?

- [ ] Any plane that failed its criteria, or any suspected cardiac abnormality [1]
- [ ] Persistent rate of 110 or below, or 180 or above, or frequent or persistent irregular rhythm [5]
- [ ] Ventricles unequal in mid-gestation, or great arteries clearly unequal [7, 8]
- [ ] Heart or stomach not on the left; abnormal axis [10, 9]
- [ ] Extracardiac anomaly associated with heart disease, hydrops, or a genetic abnormality [5]
- [ ] Nuchal translucency was 3.5 mm or more [6]
- [ ] Maternal or family indication present: first-degree relative, pregestational diabetes, anti-Ro/SSA, phenylketonuria, retinoids, confirmed fetal infection [11]
